title: Pediatric Asthma Exacerbation — Severity & Management
keywords: this is the older wheezing child, distinct from bronchiolitis which is the under-2 first-time-wheeze picture with a different treatment approach entirely, don't treat a toddler's asthma exacerbation like bronchiolitis or vice versa
PRAM scores oxygen saturation, suprasternal retractions, scalene muscle use, air entry, and wheezing, 0-12, higher is worse, validated ages 2-17
the treatment ladder escalates by how the child responds to the last step, not by a fixed time interval alone, reassess after every intervention
back-to-back or continuous nebulized albuterol for moderate-severe exacerbations, not spaced-out single treatments, and add ipratropium in the same nebulizer for the first few doses

purpose: Severity assessment (PRAM) and the stepwise bronchodilator/steroid/magnesium escalation ladder for a pediatric asthma exacerbation — the older-child wheeze picture, distinct from infant bronchiolitis.
ageRange: Roughly 2-17 years — PRAM is validated in this range. A first-time wheeze under age 2 is more likely bronchiolitis (see bronchiolitis-management) and is managed differently.

body.text: This is the OLDER child with known or new asthma — distinct from bronchiolitis (typically under 2, first-time wheeze, viral etiology, bronchodilators/steroids are NOT the mainstay per bronchiolitis-management). Don't apply this module's ladder to a bronchiolitis presentation or vice versa — the two conditions look superficially similar (a wheezing child) but have different evidence-based treatment approaches.

The Pediatric Respiratory Assessment Measure (PRAM) is a validated bedside score (ages 2-17) combining oxygen saturation, suprasternal retractions, scalene muscle use, air entry, and wheezing into a 0-12 scale (higher = more severe). It's most useful for tracking TREND — reassessing before and after treatment to gauge response — rather than as a single static number to act on in isolation. A high PRAM score is a strong predictor of hospital admission.
Stepwise treatment ladder — escalate by RESPONSE, not a fixed timer

items: MILD exacerbations: intermittent nebulized (or MDI-with-spacer) albuterol, spaced doses, reassess response before deciding on disposition.

MODERATE-SEVERE exacerbations: BACK-TO-BACK or CONTINUOUS nebulized albuterol rather than spaced single treatments — this is a meaningful escalation in intensity, not just repeating the mild-exacerbation approach more often. Add nebulized IPRATROPIUM to the albuterol for the first several doses in moderate-severe presentations — combination therapy in the acute phase has better evidence than albuterol alone at this severity.

Systemic corticosteroids (oral or IV — oral is equally effective if the child can tolerate it and isn't vomiting) given EARLY for any exacerbation beyond mild, not held in reserve — steroids take hours to have clinical effect, so early administration matters for their eventual benefit to be realized during the ED visit/admission.

IV MAGNESIUM SULFATE for severe exacerbations not adequately responding to the above — this is a genuinely evidence-supported step with real bronchodilator effect, not a last-ditch or purely 'nothing else to try' measure. Don't skip past it or delay it while cycling through more albuterol alone in a child who's already severe and not improving.

Reassess after EVERY intervention and let the child's response (not a fixed time interval) drive the next escalation decision — a child not improving after back-to-back albuterol plus ipratropium plus steroids plus magnesium is in genuinely severe/refractory status and needs escalating respiratory support and ICU-level care.

Terbutaline (subcutaneous or IV) and other second-line agents are used in refractory cases per institutional protocol/ICU involvement — this is beyond typical ED-only management and usually accompanies escalating respiratory support.

body.text:
A child who is not responding to the medication ladder and is showing worsening work of breathing, fatigue, or declining mental status needs escalating respiratory support:
- high-flow nasal cannula or noninvasive ventilation as a bridge in appropriate candidates
- intubation reserved for true respiratory failure or impending arrest, given that positive-pressure ventilation in status asthmaticus carries real risk (breath-stacking, barotrauma, hemodynamic compromise from high intrathoracic pressure in an obstructed lung)

If intubation and mechanical ventilation become necessary, see status-asthmaticus-ventilation for the specific 'minimize minute ventilation, tolerate permissive hypercapnia' strategy that obstructive lung physiology requires — this is deliberately NOT restated here since that module already covers it in depth.
